newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Pressure on Canberra to drop euthanasia challenge.
newsitem.headline: Pressure on Canberra to drop euthanasia challenge.

text.p: Australia's parliament faced mounting pressure on Sunday to reject a move to overturn the world's first law legalising mercy killings.

A leading figure in conservative Prime Minister John Howard's ruling Liberal Party, Victorian state government chief Jeff Kennett, said politicians had no right to intefere in citizen's private lives.

"I think most Australians support the view that I put -- I cannot understand why the federal parliament is involving itself in this argument," Kennett said in a television interview. "This is being driven, unfortunately, by an individual who has a view which is in my opinion totally wrong."
Australia's outback Northern Territory introduced the world's first voluntary euthanasia law earlier this year, sparking controversy around the country and overseas.

Government backbencher Kevin Andrews, with Howard's support, has launched a private bid in the national parliament to have Canberra use its constitutional powers to overturn the territory's law, which came into effect in July.

The first death under the law last Sunday of 66-year-old former carpenter and one-time Christian missionary Bob Dent has sparked emotional debate among Australians about whether assisted suicide should be legalised, or whether the terminally-ill should be forced to continue suffering until they die naturally.
Political leaders, including Howard and his deputy, Tim Fischer, have urged the repeal of the territory's law, which critics condemn as legalised killing.
But various opinion polls show strong public support, with up to eight in 10 Australians in favour.
The doctor who helped Dent to die, euthanasia campaigner Philip Nitschke, backed Kennett's call.
"There is no place for a federal directive on this issue," he told Reuters.
"This is overwhelmingly popular in the community and the politicians should keep that in mind."
Kennett described Dent's death as "beautiful".
"I think Mr Dent's passing was beautiful for him, it must have been beautiful for his family," he said.
"For Mr Andrews and anyone else to impose their will on how an individual wants to conduct his or her life after every other form of assistance has failed, I think, is morally wrong."

Opinion in the territory appears to run strongly in favour of the law and the territory government's right to pass it, with public phone-ins to radio stations and letters to the local newspaper showing overwhelming support.
The architect of the assisted-suicide law, former territory government chief Marshall Perron also urged Australians to lobby their national parliamentarians to reject the Andrews move.
Perron said politicians risked being swayed by the vocal anti-euthanasia lobby and ignoring the overwhelming popular support for voluntary euthanasia.
"The opponents scare politicians, but the supporters do not," Perron told Reuters.
"Every Australian should write to their federal members and senators protesting and asking them to back off."
The law is also facing a separate challenge in the High Court. A coalition of doctors, church and Aboriginal leaders has petitioned the country's highest court to declare the law unconstitutional.
